label: thm:calibration
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Exact calibration

label: lem:mean-identity
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Determinant and mean identities

title: Proof
body_md:
Expand the determinant into distinct rank-one row contributions. A term
using $k$ rows belongs to $\binom{m-k}{s-k}$ size-$s$ subsets. Summing in
$s$ proves \eqref{eq:partition-generating}. For the mean, allow nonsymmetric
rank-one contributions and replace $x_ix_i^\top$ by
$x_i(x_i+t y_i v)^\top$. On a selected subset the derivative at zero is
$\det(G_S+R)v^\top(G_S+R)^{-1}X_S^\top y_S$. On the total Gram matrix
the derivative is $v^\top(\nabla_G Z_s)X^\top y$. Equating these
derivatives and dividing by $Z_s$ proves \eqref{eq:mean-identity}.
head: environment

label: lem:moment-map
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:moment-map}
Let $1\le s\le m$ and $m\ge d$. The gradient of
$A_s(z)=\log P_s(e^z)$, with $P_s$ in \eqref{eq:cal-partition}, is a
bijection onto
$\{\rho:0<\rho_j<1,\ \sum_j\rho_j<s\}$.
head: environment
name: Finite inverse moment map

title: Proof
body_md:
The distribution on $J\subseteq[d]$ with mass proportional to
$c_{|J|}\exp(\sum_{j\in J}z_j)$ has support all zero-one vectors with at
most $s$ ones. Its convex hull is
$\mathcal C_s=\{\rho:0\le\rho_j\le1,\ \sum_j\rho_j\le s\}$.
To check the hull, any vertex with two fractional coordinates admits a
feasible perturbation; a vertex with one fractional coordinate cannot
satisfy an active integral sum constraint and also admits a perturbation.
Thus every vertex is a stated zero-one vector.

The gradient of $A_s$ is the mean indicator, and its Hessian is the
indicator covariance. A zero-variance linear combination must agree on
the empty set and every singleton, so all its coefficients are zero.
The Hessian is therefore positive definite. Every finite parameter gives
positive probability to every support point, so its mean is interior.
Conversely, for an interior $\rho$, a ball of radius $\delta>0$ about
$\rho$ lies in $\mathcal C_s$. The support function then gives
\[
 A_s(z)-\rho^\top z\ge\delta\lVert z\rVert+
             \min_{k:c_k>0}\log c_k.
\]
This function is coercive and strictly convex. Its unique minimizer
solves $\nabla A_s(z)=\rho$. This also proves injectivity. When a sum
constraint is redundant, the displayed strict inequality remains true
through $0<\rho_j<1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use coefficient coordinates $\widetilde w=G^{1/2}w$ and design
$\widetilde X=XG^{-1/2}$, whose Gram matrix is $I$. Write
\[
 C=G^{-1/2}RG^{-1/2},\qquad
 D=G^{1/2}(G+A_0)^{-1}G^{1/2},\qquad 0\prec D\prec I.
\]
If $C=U\operatorname{diag}(c_j)U^\top$, put $q_j=1/c_j$. The
determinant expansion gives $Z_s(I,C)=\det(C)P_s(q)$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:mean-identity} gives the mean operator
\[
 \Phi_s(C)\widetilde X^\top,\qquad
 \Phi_s(C)=U\operatorname{diag}(\rho_j(q))U^\top.
\]
The desired operator is $D\widetilde X^\top$. Full row rank of
$\widetilde X^\top$ makes calibration equivalent to $\Phi_s(C)=D$.
Thus every solution $C$ commutes with $D$. In a simultaneous eigenbasis,
Lemma~\ref{lem:moment-map} gives exactly one positive eigenvalue vector
$q$ if and only if $\operatorname{tr}D<s$. Equal target eigenvalues
force equal $q$ coordinates, since swapping them preserves the unique
moment-map solution. There is no freedom to rotate a different penalty
inside a repeated eigenspace. This proves all-matrix uniqueness and
\eqref{eq:feasibility}. Equivalently, the exact identity
\[
 \rho_i-\rho_j=\frac{q_i-q_j}{P_s(q)}
 \sum_{J\subseteq[d]\setminus\{i,j\}}c_{|J|+1}\prod_{k\in J}q_k
\]
has a strictly positive final factor, whose empty term is $c_1>0$.
Unwhitening gives $R_s=G^{1/2}CG^{1/2}$. For scalar $A_0$, $D$ is a
spectral function of $G$, so $R_s$ commutes with $G$.

For the bounds, write $q_J=\prod_{k\in J}q_k$ and split
$P_s=B_j+q_jA_j$. Then
\[
 \frac{\rho_j}{1-\rho_j}=q_j\frac{A_j}{B_j},\qquad
 \frac{A_j}{B_j}
 =\frac{\sum_{J\not\ni j}c_{|J|}q_J (s-|J|)/(m-|J|)}
        {\sum_{J\not\ni j}c_{|J|}q_J}.
\]
Terms with zero coefficient are omitted. At $s<m$ all denominators here
are positive; this weighted average is at most $s/m$. For $s\ge d$ it lies between
$(s-d+1)/(m-d+1)$ and $s/m$. The eigenvalues of the whitened target
penalty are $(1-\rho_j)/\rho_j$, and the ratio of the calibrated to
target eigenvalues is $A_j/B_j$. Congruence proves
\eqref{eq:penalty-upper} and \eqref{eq:penalty-sandwich}. If $d>1$ and
$d\le s<m$, the positive weights at $|J|=0$ and $|J|=d-1$ have distinct
ratios, so both sandwich inequalities are strict. At $s=m$ the fit is deterministic; equality
of its operator with the target and full rank give $R_m=A_0$ directly.
head: environment

label: cor:calibration-closed
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Two closed forms

title: Proof
body_md:
For $s=1$, $P_1(q)=m+\sum_jq_j$. Hence
$q_j=m\rho_j/(1-\sum_k\rho_k)$.
In the whitened coordinates of the theorem, this says
$C=(1-\operatorname{tr}D)D^{-1}/m$.
Congruence by $G^{1/2}$ proves \eqref{eq:singleton-penalty}.
For $d=1$, $P_s(q)=c_0+c_1q$ and $c_1/c_0=s/m$.
The odds equation in the theorem's proof gives $r_s=s\lambda_0/m$.
head: environment

label: lem:zero-variance
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:zero-variance}
Let $d\ge2$, $1\le s<m$, and $R\succ0$. Under any law positive on
every size-$s$ subset, the selected ridge fits satisfy
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(w_S)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_i y_i=0\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
Thus the zero-variance responses are exactly those supported on zero rows.
This statement does not require calibration.
head: environment
name: Zero total variance

title: Proof
body_md:
Zero covariance makes all fits the same vector $w$. Set
$v_i=x_i(y_i-x_i^\top w)$. The normal equations give
$\sum_{i\in S}v_i=Rw$ for every size-$s$ subset.
For any two indices, choose $s-1$ other indices and exchange the remaining
index. This shows that all $v_i$ agree. Their common value lies in every
row line. Those lines have zero intersection because the rows span at
least two dimensions. Hence $v_i=0$ and $Rw=0$, so $w=0$ and $x_iy_i=0$.
The converse follows because every selected right-hand side is then zero.
head: environment

label: prop:common-energy
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:common-energy}
Let $d\ge2$. At every feasible $1\le s<m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:common-energy-bound}
 0<\underline c_s\le\overline c_s<\infty,\qquad
 \underline c_s\mathcal E_0(y)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_s(y)
 \le\overline c_s\mathcal E_0(y).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for any two feasible interior budgets $s,t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:total-comparison}
 \frac{\underline c_s}{\overline c_t}\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_t(y)
 \le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_s(y)
 \le\frac{\overline c_s}{\underline c_t}\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_t(y).
\end{equation}
For a fixed $W\succ0$, the same comparison holds for
$\operatorname{tr}(W\Sigma_s)$ after multiplying the lower constant by
$\lambda_{\min}(W)/\lambda_{\max}(W)$ and the upper constant by its
reciprocal. The energy $\mathcal E_0$ vanishes exactly on the zero-row
response space.
head: environment
name: Common-energy comparison

label: eq:uniform-energy
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\delta_S=w_S-w_0$. The selected normal equation gives
\[
 (G_S+R_s)\delta_S=\sum_{i\in S}b_i-R_sw_0=:t_S.
\]
Let $U_s$ be the uniform law on size-$s$ subsets. Write
$t_S=\sum_{i\in S}(b_i-\bar b)+[(s/m)A_0-R_s]w_0$.
Uniform inclusion probabilities are $s/m$ for one index and
$s(s-1)/[m(m-1)]$ for two distinct indices. Since
$\sum_i(b_i-\bar b)=0$, expansion yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-energy}
 \mathbb E_{U_s}\lVert t_S\rVert^2
 =a_s\mathcal E_0+\lVert[(s/m)A_0-R_s]w_0\rVert^2.
\end{equation}
For a nonzero row, $b_i$ belongs to its row line. Projection onto the
orthogonal complement of that line therefore gives
\[
 \lVert b_i-\bar b\rVert^2\ge
 \frac{\lVert x_i\rVert^2\lVert\bar b\rVert^2-(x_i^\top\bar b)^2}{L_x^2}.
\]
For a zero row the right side is zero. Summing and using the largest
eigenvalue of $G$ gives
\[
 \mathcal E_0\ge\mu_X\lVert\bar b\rVert^2,\qquad
 \lVert A_0w_0\rVert^2\le\frac{m^2}{\mu_X}\mathcal E_0.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:uniform-energy} lies between $a_s\mathcal E_0$ and
$(a_s+m^2\lVert \mathcal D_s\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2/\mu_X)\mathcal E_0$.

The order bounds $R_s\preceq G_S+R_s\preceq G+R_s$ imply
\[
 \frac{\lVert t_S\rVert}{\Lambda_s}\le\lVert\delta_S\rVert
 \le\frac{\lVert t_S\rVert}{r_{\min,s}}.
\]
Every determinant weight lies between $\det R_s$ and $\det(G+R_s)$.
Its ratio to the average weight therefore lies between
$\kappa_s^{-1}$ and $\kappa_s$, so
$\kappa_s^{-1}\le p_{s,R_s}(S)/U_s(S)\le\kappa_s$.
Calibration gives $\mathbb E_p\delta_S=0$ and hence
$\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_s=\mathbb E_p\lVert\delta_S\rVert^2$.
Combining the bounds proves \eqref{eq:common-energy-bound}.
Combining budgets proves \eqref{eq:total-comparison}; the extreme
eigenvalues of $W$ prove its query version.
Lemma~\ref{lem:zero-variance} identifies the common zero space.
head: environment

label: thm:loo-envelope
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:loo-envelope}
Under the preceding assumptions, $\rho>0$. The risk satisfies
$h_{m-1}(X,W)\le\rho$.
The equality kernel at this envelope is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loo-kernel}
 \ker(\rho K-C_{m-1})
 =\{y:X^\top y=0,\ y_i=0\text{ for }i\notin M\}.
\end{equation}
Thus $h_{m-1}(X,W)=\rho$ if and only if the rows $X_M$ are linearly
dependent. When this holds, \eqref{eq:loo-kernel} is the complete
maximizing space, of dimension $|M|-\operatorname{rank}(X_M)$.
If those rows are independent, $h_{m-1}(X,W)<\rho$.
head: environment
name: LOO envelope and attainment

label: eq:loo-deletion
title: Proof
body_md:
Every deleted normal matrix $G+R-x_ix_i^\top$ is positive definite.
The determinant lemma and the rank-one inverse identity give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loo-deletion}
 0\le\ell_i<1,\qquad p_i=\frac{1-\ell_i}{D},\qquad
 w_{-i}=BX^\top y-\frac{Bx_i(Ly)_i}{1-\ell_i}.
\end{equation}
Also $D=m-\operatorname{tr}(GB)>m-d\ge1$.
The mean of the deleted correction is $D^{-1}BX^\top Ly$.
Since $X^\top L=RBX^\top$, all-response calibration and full row rank
of $X^\top$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loo-calibration-identity}
 (G+A_0)^{-1}=B-D^{-1}BRB,\qquad
 K-L=D^{-1}XBRBX^\top.
\end{equation}
The second matrix is positive semidefinite with kernel $\ker(X^\top)$.
No commutation is used here.

Taking the correction's second moment in \eqref{eq:loo-deletion} and
subtracting its mean square gives the centered response operator
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loo-centered-operator}
 C_{m-1}=L\operatorname{diag}(\omega_i)L
       -D^{-2}LXBWBX^\top L.
\end{equation}
Woodbury gives $L=(I+XR^{-1}X^\top)^{-1}$, so $0\prec L\preceq I$.
Spectral calculus for this matrix gives $L-L^2\succeq0$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loo-full-gap}
 K-L^2=(K-L)+(L-L^2)\succeq0,\qquad
 \ker(K-L^2)=\ker(X^\top).
\end{equation}
Since the vectors $Bx_i$ span coefficient space and $W\ne0$, at least
one $v_i=\lVert W^{1/2}Bx_i\rVert^2$ is positive. Hence $\rho>0$.
Combining the identities gives the exact deficit
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loo-deficit-main}
 \rho K-C_{m-1}=\rho(K-L^2)
   +L\operatorname{diag}(\rho-\omega_i)L
   +D^{-2}LXBWBX^\top L.
\end{equation}
All three terms are positive semidefinite. The first forces
$X^\top y=0$ at equality. Then $Ly=y$, the last term vanishes, and the
middle term vanishes exactly when $y$ is supported on $M$.
This proves \eqref{eq:loo-kernel}. Such responses identify with
$\ker(X_M^\top)$, giving the dimension and attainment criterion.
If the dimension is zero, the deficit is positive definite. Compactness
of $\{y:y^\top Ky=1\}$ then gives $h_{m-1}(X,W)<\rho$.
head: environment

label: cor:loo-balance
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:loo-balance}
If $v_i/(1-\ell_i)=a$ for every row, then $a>0$,
$h_{m-1}(X,W)=a/D$, and the complete maximizing space is $\ker(X^\top)$.
Conversely, if every nonzero residual response globally maximizes risk,
then $\omega_i=h_{m-1}(X,W)$ on each non-coloop row.
Here a \emph{coloop} is a row whose deletion lowers column rank.
If there are no coloops, the following conditions are equivalent:
constant scores; every nonzero residual maximizes; and the complete
maximizing space is $\ker(X^\top)$.
head: environment
name: Combined balance and the coloop qualification

title: Proof
body_md:
Constant scores make $M$ contain every row, and $m>d$ guarantees a
nonzero residual. The theorem proves the forward statement.
For the converse write $h=h_{m-1}(X,W)$. At any global maximizer $z$,
Rayleigh stationarity gives $C_{m-1}z=hKz$. For residual $z$, $Lz=Kz=z$,
and the centered term in \eqref{eq:loo-centered-operator} vanishes.
Hence $L\operatorname{diag}(\omega_i)z=hz$.
Multiplying by $L^{-1}$ gives $\operatorname{diag}(\omega_i)z=hz$.
Row $i$ is not a coloop exactly when some residual has $z_i\ne0$:
a dependence with that nonzero coefficient expresses row $i$ using the
others, and conversely. Thus $\omega_i=h$ on every such row.
With no coloops this proves constancy and the stated equivalence.

label: prop:loo-matrix-contact
title: Proposition

name: Calibrated LOO matrix contact

label: thm:sharp-geometry
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Sharp query risk and all maximizers

label: eq:sharp-deficit
title: Proof
body_md:
The strict signs determine the sharp value and every maximizing response
through the exact deficit
\begin{align}\label{eq:sharp-deficit}
 \alpha_scJ_0-\operatorname{tr}(W\Sigma_s)
 ={}&\alpha_s\sum_j(c-W_{jj})E_j\nonumber\\
 &+b\sum_j(\alpha_sc-\beta_sW_{jj})q_j^2\nonumber\\
 &+b\tau_sq^\top Wq.
\end{align}
Every mean coefficient is strictly positive. Equality therefore forces
all group means to vanish and all contrasts to lie in $I_{\max}$.
Conversely those responses attain the bound. Off-diagonal entries of
$W$ affect individual risks but neither the sharp value nor this space.

The hard step is the strict sign $\alpha_s>\beta_s$, including middle
budgets. Its proof is computer-assisted and exact. Deletion identities
reduce it to a reciprocal moment. A variance bound places an auxiliary
mean above a quadratic root. Two reciprocal lower bounds cover different
parts of the root domain, and finite integer polynomial certificates
prove the needed signs and monotonicity on that entire domain.
Here are the precise reductions used by that sign proof. For
$g(x)=(1+x)^{n-1}[r+(r+n)x]$, put
\[
\begin{split}
 Z&=[x^s]g(x)^d,\quad
 Q=[x^s](1+x)^{d(n-1)+1}[r+(r+n)x]^{d-1},\\
 T&=[x^{s-1}](1+x)^{d(n-1)}[r+(r+n)x]^{d-2},\\
 A&=[x^{s-1}]g(x)^{d-1}
       \sum_{j=0}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{j}\frac{x^j}{r+1+j}.
\end{split}
\]
Deletion of one or two determinant factors gives
$\alpha=A/Z$ and $\beta=[nT-(n-1)A]/[(n+r)Q]$.
Thus it suffices to prove $A\{(n+r)Q+(n-1)Z\}>nZT$.
For $n\ge3,d\ge4$, select $s-1$ items with product weights from
$d(n-1)$ weight-one items and $d-2$ items of weight $(r+n)/r$.
For disjoint ordinary blocks of sizes $n-2,n$, with counts $U,V$,
coefficient extraction gives $A/T=\mathbb E[(r+V)/(r+1+U)]$.
Two lower bounds are used: the pointwise integer bound
\[
 \frac1{r+1+U}\ge\frac{r+2-U}{(r+1)(r+2)}
\]
and weighted Cauchy. The variance of the number of unselected
exceptional items places its mean above the positive root of an explicit
quadratic. At that root, three rational cells cover the full domain.
On the two lower cells the integer bound has positive residual; on the
upper cell Cauchy does. Exact positive-coefficient expansions also prove
the monotonicity needed to pass from the root to the actual mean.
Appendix~\ref{app:geometry} gives every defining polynomial, the cell
maps and their inverses, both finite seams, and the minimum-budget face.
It also proves the separate $n=2$ and $d=2,3$ cases, and the direct LOO
endpoint. These cases cover exactly the theorem's domain. Newton's
coefficient inequality gives strict negative covariance of the increasing
count scores, hence $\tau>0$; its boundary-aware conditional argument is
included there. All large coefficient checks use exact integer arithmetic.
The preceding deficit then proves the theorem.
head: environment

label: prop:small-penalty-gap
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:small-penalty-gap}
In the balanced model with $n,d\ge2$ and $s=d$, if the calibrated raw
penalty satisfies $0<r_d\le1/(4d^2)$, then
\[
 \alpha_d-\beta_d\ge\frac1{4[d(n-1)+1]}.
\]
For fixed $n,d$, as the raw penalty $r\downarrow0$ and the induced target
also tends to zero,
\[
 \alpha\longrightarrow\frac1n,\qquad
 \beta\longrightarrow\frac{(n-1)(d-1)}{n[d(n-1)+1]},\qquad
 \frac{\lambda_0}{r}\longrightarrow d(n-1)+1.
\]
head: environment
name: Minimum-budget margin

label: eq:margin-reduction
title: Proof
body_md:
Put $M=d(n-1)$ and use the deletion quantities $A,Q,T,Z$ from the
preceding proof at $s=d$. In the auxiliary experiment, the number $H$
of unselected exceptional items has mass proportional to
\[
 \binom{d-2}{j}\binom M{j+1}\left(\frac r{r+n}\right)^j,
 \qquad 0\le j\le d-2.
\]
The ordinary selected count is $1+H$. Write $h=\mathbb EH$, and let
$U,V$ count disjoint ordinary blocks of sizes $n-2,n$. Define
\begin{align*}
 Q_n&=rnd(nd-1)+nd(M+1)+n^2dh,\\
 Z_n&=rQ_n+nd[r(nd-1)+n(1+h)],\\
 H_n&=(n+r)Q_n+(n-1)Z_n,\\
 B&=Mr+n(1+h),\qquad C=Mr(d-1)-(1+h)r(d-1).
\end{align*}
Adding the deleted factors and taking ordinary factorial moments gives
\[
 \frac QT=\frac{Q_n}{dM},\quad \frac ZT=\frac{Z_n}{dM},\quad
 \mathbb E(r+V)=\frac BM,\quad
 \mathbb E[(r+V)U]=\frac{(n-2)C}{M(M-1)}.
\]
These are also the specialization $u=1$ of
\eqref{eq:actual-mean-identities}; they remain valid when $n=2$ or $d=2$.
The integer reciprocal bound gives
\[
 \frac AT\ge
 \frac{(r+2)(M-1)B-(n-2)C}{M(M-1)(r+1)(r+2)}.
\]
Consequently, if
\[
 P(h)=[(r+2)(M-1)B-(n-2)C]H_n
       -n(r+1)(r+2)M(M-1)Z_n,
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:margin-reduction}
 \alpha-\beta\ge
 \frac{dP(h)}{(M-1)(r+1)(r+2)(n+r)Q_nZ_n}.
\end{equation}
The short expansions in Appendix~\ref{app:margin-algebra} show that
$P(h)=P(0)+p_1h+p_2h^2$, with $p_1,p_2>0$, and
\[
 P(0)\ge dn^4(M-1)[2-d^2(3r+4r^2+r^3)].
\]
On the stated window the subtracted expression is at most
$3/4+1/16+1/1024<1$. Hence $P(h)\ge dn^4(M-1)$.

The adjacent mass ratio for $H$ gives the drift identity
\[
 r(d-2)(M-1)=r(nd-2)h+nh+n\mathbb EH^2.
\]
Since $H^2\ge H$, we obtain
$0\le h\le r(d-2)(M-1)/(2n)\le rd^2/2\le1/8$.
For $Q_0=nd(M+1)$ and $Z_0=n^2d$, it follows that
\begin{align*}
 Q_n/Q_0
 &=1+\frac{r(nd-1)+nh}{M+1}
 \le1+2r+r(d-2)/2\le1+rd\le9/8,\\
 Z_n/Z_0
 &=1+h+\frac{r(nd-1)}n+
          \frac{r(M+1)}n\frac{Q_n}{Q_0}
 \le1+\frac18+\frac{17}8rd<\frac32,\\
 \frac{(r+1)(r+2)(n+r)}{2n}
 &\le\frac{17}{16}\left(\frac{33}{32}\right)^2
 =\frac{18513}{16384}.
\end{align*}
Here $(nd-1)/(M+1)\le2$, $(M+1)/n\le d$, $rd\le1/8$,
and $r\le1/16$ were used. Substitution into
\eqref{eq:margin-reduction} yields
\[
 \alpha-\beta\ge
 \frac1{M+1}\frac{1/2}{(18513/16384)(9/8)(3/2)}
 =\frac{131072}{499851(M+1)}>\frac1{4(M+1)}.
\]
Finally, the coefficient definitions at $r=0$ give
$Z=n^d$, $A=n^{d-1}$, $Q=n^{d-1}(M+1)$, and $T=n^{d-2}M$.
Their positive denominators give the asserted limits, including
$\alpha-\beta\to1/(M+1)$. Since $b=nrQ/Z$ and
$\lambda_0=nb/(n-b)$, also $\lambda_0/r\to M+1$.

label: thm:etf-triple
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:etf-triple}
Under the preceding assumptions, every prescribed $\lambda_0>0$ has
exactly one calibrated positive scalar penalty, also unique among all SPD
penalties. The centered isotropic response operator is
\[
 C_{m-3}(X,I)=c_R(I-P)+c_FP,\qquad
 K_X=(I-P)+k_FP,\quad k_F=\frac{\lambda_0}{g+\lambda_0}.
\]
For every positive $r$, $c_Rk_F-c_F>0$ and $c_F\ge0$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-deficit}
 h_{m-3}(X,wI)=wc_R,\qquad
 wc_RK_X-C_{m-3}(X,wI)=w(c_Rk_F-c_F)P.
\end{equation}
The complete maximizing response space is $\ker(X^\top)$, of dimension
$m-d$. Every response with a nonzero fitted component has strictly
smaller normalized risk.
head: environment
name: Isotropic ETF geometry at three deletions

title: Proof
body_md:
\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Triangle classes and positivity.}
For a deleted triple $D_0=\{i,j,l\}$ put
$e=\operatorname{sign}(T_{ij}T_{jl}T_{li})\in\{-1,1\}$.
A diagonal sign switch makes the three off-diagonal entries of its local
Gram $J=E_{D_0}TE_{D_0}^\top$ all equal to $e\mu$.
Thus $J$ has eigenvalues $1+2e\mu,1-e\mu,1-e\mu$.
The retained Gram has eigenvalues $g$ repeated $d-3$ times,
$g-1-2e\mu$ once, and $g-1+e\mu$ twice. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-det}
 \det(G_S+rI)=z^{d-3}\delta_e,\qquad
 \delta_e=(h-2e\mu)(h+e\mu)^2=h^3-3hq-2e\mu^3.
\end{equation}
The $(i,j)$ entry of $T^2=gT$, multiplied by $T_{ij}$, gives
\[
 \sum_{l\ne i,j}T_{ij}T_{il}T_{jl}=(g-2)q.
\]
Hence the number of type-$e$ triples through every pair, through every
vertex, and in total is respectively
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-incidence}
 n_e=\frac{m-2+e(g-2)/\mu}{2},\quad
 \nu_e=\frac{(m-1)n_e}{2},\quad N_e=\frac{m(m-1)n_e}{6}.
\end{equation}
Both classes occur, since
\[
 (m-2)^2q-(g-2)^2=\frac{m^2(d-1)(k-1)}{d^2(m-1)}>0.
\]
With $N=\binom m3$, summing \eqref{eq:triple-det} yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-law}
 Z_s(r)=Nz^{d-3}D,\qquad
 \mathbb P(S=D_0^c)=\frac{\delta_e}{ND}.
\end{equation}
All triples in one class have the same individual probability.
This probability differs between the two classes.

Every retained Gram is positive definite even at $r=0$. For $k\ge4$,
\[
 (g-1)^2-4q=\frac{k[(k-4)d+k(k-1)]}{d^2(m-1)}>0.
\]
For $k=3$, complete the columns of $X/\sqrt g$ to an orthogonal matrix
and multiply its remaining columns by $\sqrt{m/k}$. This gives a unit-row
ETF in dimension three. Its row projectors have positive definite
Frobenius Gram matrix $(1-q')I+q'\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top$, with $q'<1$,
so they are linearly independent in the six-dimensional space of
symmetric $3$ by $3$ matrices. Therefore $m\le6$. Since $d\ge3$, the
only possible pair is $d=k=3$, where $(g-1)^2-4q=1/5$.
Thus $g-1>2\mu$ in every actual case. In particular $z$,
$h\pm2\mu$, $\delta_e$, $D$, and $h^2-4q$ are positive.
This is the usual Naimark-complement and projector-dimension argument;
it does not assert existence at other formal parameter pairs.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Calibration with the target fixed first.}
Expanding the selected determinants into original-row minors and counting
the supersets of each minor gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-partition}
 Z_s(X,r)=\sum_{j=0}^d\binom{m-j}{s-j}r^{d-j}e_j(X^\top X).
\end{equation}
At $X^\top X=gI$, the matrix derivative of $\log Z_s$ with respect to
the Gram is scalar. Differentiating instead with respect to each original
row identifies the entire mean map as $f(r)X^\top$. Taking the trace of
its product with $X$ gives
\[
 mf(r)=\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}[G_S(G_S+rI)^{-1}]
       =d-rZ_s'(r)/Z_s(r)=M(r).
\]
Every coefficient in \eqref{eq:triple-partition} is positive, because
$s=m-3\ge d$. Under the distribution on $j$ proportional to those
terms, $M=\mathbb E j$ and
\[
 \frac{dM}{d\log r}=-\operatorname{Var}(j)<0,\qquad
 M(0+)=d,\quad M(+\infty)=0.
\]
Thus $M/m=1/(g+\lambda_0)$ has a unique positive solution for every
fixed positive target. Theorem~\ref{thm:calibration} gives uniqueness
among SPD penalties. In particular $k_F=1-M/d=rH_1/d>0$.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The centered operator has two sectors.}
Put $L=I-T/z$ and $Q_{D_0}=I_3-J/z$. Solving the retained normal equation
gives
\[
 w_S=z^{-1}X^\top y-z_{D_0}(y),\qquad
 z_{D_0}(y)=z^{-1}X_{D_0}^\top Q_{D_0}^{-1}E_{D_0}Ly.
\]
The mean correction is $(z^{-1}-f)X^\top y$. To compute its second moment,
put $a=e\mu$ and define
\begin{align*}
 A_e&=\frac{z^2(1+a-2q)(a-2h)}{(h-2a)^2(h+a)^2},\\
 B_e&=\frac{z^2(h^2+2h-a+2q)}{(h-2a)^2(h+a)^2}.
\end{align*}
Interpolation of $z^2x/(z-x)^2$ at $1+2a,1-a$ gives
$Q_{D_0}^{-1}JQ_{D_0}^{-1}=A_eI_3+B_eJ$.
Its diagonal entries are $A_e+B_e$, and its $(i,j)$ entry is $B_eT_{ij}$.
Using the exact probabilities and the incidences in
\eqref{eq:triple-incidence}, its embedded average is $A_*I+B_*T$, where
\begin{align*}
 A_*&=\frac1{ND}\sum_{e=\pm1}n_e\delta_e
       \left[\frac{m-1}{2}A_e+\frac{m-3}{2}B_e\right],\\
 B_*&=\frac1{ND}\sum_{e=\pm1}n_e\delta_e B_e.
\end{align*}
Subtracting the actual correction mean square yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-local-operator}
 C=z^{-2}L(A_*I+B_*T)L-(z^{-1}-f)^2T.
\end{equation}
Since $T$ is zero on residuals and equals $gI$ on fitted responses,
this proves the asserted two-sector form. No transitivity of a frame
symmetry group is needed.

The retained spectra and actual class weights give
$H_j=\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(G_S+rI)^{-j}$, $j=1,2$.
For example,
\begin{align*}
 \delta_e\left[\frac1{h-2a}+\frac2{h+a}\right]&=3(h^2-q),\\
 \delta_e\left[\frac1{(h-2a)^2}+\frac2{(h+a)^2}\right]
 &=\frac{3(h^2-2ha+3q)}{h-2a}.
\end{align*}
Averaging the second line gives
$3[h(h^2-q)+3t]/[(h^2-4q)D]$, proving
\eqref{eq:triple-moments}. In particular $H_2$ is not simply $-H_1'$;
the law changes with $r$.

For the original-coordinate fit map
$F_S=(G_S+rI)^{-1}X_S^\top E_S$, let $O=\mathbb EF_S^\top F_S$.
Then
\[
 \operatorname{tr}O=H_1-rH_2,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(PO)=B/g,\qquad C=O-f^2T.
\]
The first identity follows from $F_SF_S^\top=(G_S+rI)^{-1}G_S(G_S+rI)^{-1}$;
the second uses $F_SX=(G_S+rI)^{-1}G_S$.
Dividing the residual and fitted traces by $k$ and $d$ proves
\eqref{eq:triple-sectors}. Actual covariance gives $c_F\ge0$.
The term $gM^2/m^2$ is the necessary fitted mean-square subtraction.

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Strict gap and complete equality.}
Appendix~\ref{app:triple-certificate} constructs an integer polynomial
$\mathcal H(r,d,k)$ directly from these moments and proves the identity
\[
 c_Rk_F-c_F=\frac{3d^3r\mathcal H}{m\mathcal Z^2\mathcal E\mathcal F^2},
\]
with all denominator factors positive. After $d=u+3$, $k=v+4$, the
polynomial has 581 positive integer coefficients, including a positive
constant. The appendix gives its defining expression, the exact
division and the common-denominator derivation. The ancillary checker
reconstructs the polynomial before comparing every coefficient.
For the only remaining actual case $d=k=3$, the gap is
\[
 \frac{r(5r^2+10r+4)(5r^3+25r^2+30r+6)}
 {2(r+1)^2(5r^2+10r+1)(5r^2+10r+2)^2}>0.
\]
This is an exact algebraic proof on the whole stated domain.
Finally, for $y=y_R+y_F$ with residual and fitted components, the risk
ratio is
\[
 \frac{w[c_R\lVert y_R\rVert^2+c_F\lVert y_F\rVert^2]}
 {\lVert y_R\rVert^2+k_F\lVert y_F\rVert^2}.
\]
Its deficit from $wc_R$ times the denominator is
$w(c_Rk_F-c_F)\lVert y_F\rVert^2$. The coefficient is strictly positive,
and $k>0$ ensures nonzero residuals. This proves both the sharp value
and every equality case.
head: environment

label: prop:mixture
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: A finite improving mixture

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a balanced design, $d\le s<nd$, and its exactly calibrated
$r=r_s>0$. All expectations below use the actual count law
\eqref{eq:count-law}. Put $a=n/(n+\lambda_0)$,
$b=n(1-a)$, $\mu=s/d$, and $c_H=a/\mu$. Define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 h(k)=\frac1{r+k},\qquad f(k)=kh(k),\\
 \delta(k)=c_H-h(k),\qquad v(k)=k\delta(k),\\
 h_t(k)=h(k)+t\delta(k),\qquad g_t(k)=f(k)+tv(k).
 \end{gathered}
\]
The mixture is
$(w(t))_j=h_t(K_j)\sum_{i\in S\cap j}\varepsilon_i y_i$.
By symmetry every original row has inclusion probability $s/(nd)$.
Hence $\mathbb E w_H=aq=w_0$, and linearity proves
$\mathbb E w(t)=w_0$ for every real $t$.

\subsection{The covariance quadratics}
Conditional on all counts, the selected contrast sums are independent
across groups, have mean zero, and variance
$K_j(n-K_j)E_j/[n(n-1)]$. Thus, with
$\omega(k)=k(n-k)/[n(n-1)]$,
\begin{align}
 \alpha(t)&=\mathbb E[\omega(K_1)h_t(K_1)^2],\nonumber\\
 \beta(t)&=\frac{\mathbb E[(g_t(K_1)-g_t(K_2))^2]}{2b},\qquad
 \tau(t)=-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(g_t(K_1),g_t(K_2))}{b},\label{eq:mixture-coeff}\\
 \operatorname{Cov}(w(t))
 &=\alpha(t)\operatorname{diag}(E_j)
      +b\beta(t)\operatorname{diag}(q_j^2)-b\tau(t)qq^\top.\nonumber
\end{align}
This calculation includes the covariance between the ridge and
inclusion-weighted estimates on their shared subset. Their cross
contrast coefficient is $c_H\mathbb E[\omega(K_1)h(K_1)]$;
their mean cross covariance is
$\operatorname{Cov}(f(K_i),c_HK_j)$.
Exchangeability makes that cross covariance symmetric. No independence
between the two estimates is assumed.

For $0\le t\le1$, the score is strictly increasing:
\[
 \frac d{dk}g_t(k)=\frac{(1-t)r}{(r+k)^2}+tc_H>0.
\]
The actual-law conditional ordering proved at the start of
Appendix~\ref{app:geometry} therefore gives $\tau(t)>0$ throughout
this interval.

The positive marginal support of $K_1$ is
$\max(1,s-(d-1)n),\ldots,\min(n,s)$.
It contains two consecutive positive integers: if its upper endpoint is
$n$, then $n-1$ is possible since $s<nd$; otherwise the upper endpoint
is $s\ge2$ and the lower positive endpoint is one.
Consider the size-biased probability $\nu(k)=k\mathbb P(K_1=k)/\mu$.
Calibration says
\[
 \mathbb E_\nu h(K_1)=\frac{\mathbb E f(K_1)}\mu=c_H.
\]
Differentiating the finite sum defining $\alpha$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:negative-derivative}
 \alpha'(0)=-\frac{2\mu}{n(n-1)}
       \operatorname{Cov}_\nu((n-K_1)h(K_1),h(K_1))<0.
\end{equation}
Both functions inside this covariance are strictly decreasing on
positive counts, with derivatives $-(n+r)/(r+k)^2$ and
$-1/(r+k)^2$. The independent-copy covariance identity and the two
distinct positive support points make the covariance strictly positive.

Put
\[
 A=\alpha(0),\quad D=-\alpha'(0)>0,\quad
 Q=\mathbb E[\omega(K_1)\delta(K_1)^2].
\]
Then $\alpha(t)=A-Dt+Qt^2$. Also $Q>0$: if it vanished,
$\delta$ would vanish on every positive-$\omega$ atom, making the
derivative zero in contradiction to \eqref{eq:negative-derivative}.
Similarly,
\begin{align*}
 B_0&=\beta(0),\\
 B_1&=\mathbb E[(f(K_1)-f(K_2))(v(K_1)-v(K_2))]/b,\\
 B_2&=\mathbb E[(v(K_1)-v(K_2))^2]/(2b)\ge0,\\
 \beta(t)&=B_0+B_1t+B_2t^2.
\end{align*}
Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-geometry} supplies the strict gap $g=A-B_0>0$.
Define the finite step
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixture-step}
 H_*=D+|B_1|+Q+B_2,\qquad
 T_s=\min\left\{\frac12,\frac{D}{2Q},\frac{g}{2H_*}\right\}>0.
\end{equation}
For $0<t\le T_s$,
\[
 \alpha(t)\le A-Dt/2<A,\qquad
 \alpha(t)-\beta(t)
 \ge g-[D+|B_1|+Q+B_2]t\ge g/2>0,
\]
where $t\le1$ bounds the quadratic terms in the second inequality.
The gap, rather than a limiting continuity argument alone, gives this
explicit interval.

For $c=\max_jW_{jj}>0$, the exact deficit is
\begin{align*}
 \alpha(t)cJ_0-\operatorname{tr}(W\operatorname{Cov}(w(t)))
 ={}&\alpha(t)\sum_j(c-W_{jj})E_j\\
 &+b\sum_j[\alpha(t)c-\beta(t)W_{jj}]q_j^2
    +b\tau(t)q^\top Wq .
\end{align*}
Every mean coefficient is at least $bc[\alpha(t)-\beta(t)]>0$.
Also $\alpha(t)>0$, since an intermediate count has positive probability
and $h_t$ is positive. Equality therefore holds exactly on the same
nonzero contrast space $\mathcal E$. This proves
Proposition~\ref{prop:mixture}, including arbitrary singular and
nondiagonal PSD queries and all ties. For a finite grid of budgets,
$\min_sT_s>0$ supplies one common weight.
head: environment

label: prop:share-risk
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:share-risk}
For $0\le t\le1$ and $0\ne W\succeq0$, put
\[
 c=\max_jW_{jj},\quad p_t=\alpha(t)c,\quad
 B_t(W)=\beta(t)\operatorname{diag}(W_{jj})-\tau(t)W,\quad
 \ell_t=\lambda_{\max}(B_t(W)).
\]
The sharp value at exact share $\eta(y)=\delta$ is
$(1-\delta)p_t+\delta\ell_t$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gain-share-value}
 H_\delta(t,W)=\max\{\ell_t,(1-\delta)p_t+\delta\ell_t\}.
\end{equation}
At exact share $0<\delta<1$, all maximizers have $q$ in the complete
top eigenspace of $B_t(W)$, contrasts supported only in groups with
$W_{jj}=c$, and
$\sum_j E_j=(1-\delta)b\|q\|^2/\delta$.
At $\delta=1$ they are nonzero pure means in that eigenspace.
For the lower-bound-share class, $p_t>\ell_t$ forces share $\delta$;
$p_t<\ell_t$ forces share one; and $p_t=\ell_t$ allows every share
in $[\delta,1]$, with these same conditions on each nonzero sector.
For $W=0$, every admissible response has zero risk.
head: environment
name: Mean-share risk and all equality cases

title: Proof
body_md:
At fixed share $\eta$, the contrast and mean Rayleigh bounds give
$(1-\eta)p_t+\eta\ell_t$. Both bounds are attained independently:
$n\ge2$ supplies contrasts in every maximal group, and the mean
block has a top eigenvector. Equality in their sum requires equality
in each sector of positive energy. The function is affine in $\eta$.
Its maximum on $[\delta,1]$ and all its equality cases follow by its
slope. These sets are energy-constrained cones, generally not linear spaces.
head: environment

label: thm:share-phase
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:share-phase}
Use the feature coefficients and protected interval $0<t\le T=T_s$
in \eqref{eq:mixture-step}. Set
\[
 K_\delta=(1-\delta)D-\delta B_1,\qquad
 L_\delta=(1-\delta)Q+\delta B_2\ge0.
\]
For a fixed protected weight,
\[
 H_\delta(t,W)<H_\delta(0,W)\quad\hbox{for every }0\ne W\succeq0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K_\delta>L_\delta t.
\]
Some protected positive weight works exactly when $K_\delta>0$.
In that case one may take $t_\delta=\min\{T,K_\delta/(2L_\delta)\}$
if $L_\delta>0$, and $t_\delta=T$ otherwise.
Every protected weight works exactly when $K_\delta>L_\delta T$.
If $K_\delta\le0$, no positive scalar weight in this mixture family
improves every query, even outside the protected interval.
head: environment
name: Exact all-query improvement phase

title: Proof
body_md:
On $[0,T]$, $\alpha(t)>\beta(t)$ and $\tau(t)>0$, so
$p_t>\ell_t$ and \eqref{eq:gain-share-value} uses share $\delta$.
Put $\gamma(t)=\beta(t)-d\tau(t)$. Exchangeability gives
\[
 \gamma(t)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\sum_jg_t(K_j))}{db}
           =(1-t)^2\gamma(0)\ge0,
\]
since $\sum_jK_j=s$ is fixed. Define
$P_W=\operatorname{diag}(W_{jj})-W/d$ and $R_W=W/d$.
Both are PSD: the Gram representation of $W$ and Cauchy--Schwarz give
$W\preceq d\operatorname{diag}(W_{jj})$.
Thus $B_t(W)=\beta(t)P_W+\gamma(t)R_W$ and $P_W+R_W\preceq cI$.

Write $x=A-\alpha(t)>0$ and $y=\beta(t)-B_0$.
If $y\ge0$, the preceding identity gives
$\ell_t-\ell_0\le yc$ and hence
\[
 H_\delta(0,W)-H_\delta(t,W)
 \ge c\{(1-\delta)x-\delta y\}=ct(K_\delta-L_\delta t).
\]
A flat rank-one query $W=vv^\top$, $v_j\in\{-1,1\}$, attains this
bound: its mean top eigenspace is $v^\perp$ and $\ell_t=\beta(t)$.
This proves necessity and sufficiency when $y\ge0$.

If $y<0$, set $\rho=\max\{\beta(t)/B_0,(1-t)^2\}<1$ when
$\gamma(0)>0$, and $\rho=\beta(t)/B_0<1$ otherwise.
Here $B_0>0$ because unequal counts have positive probability and
$f$ is strictly increasing. We have $B_t(W)\preceq\rho B_0(W)$.
Also $\ell_0\ge(B_0-\tau(0))c>0$, since
$B_0-\tau(0)=((d-1)B_0+\gamma(0))/d>0$.
Consequently $\ell_t<\ell_0$ for every nonzero query. Both sectors
strictly improve, including the pure-mean class $\delta=1$.
The scalar condition holds as well because $(1-\delta)x-\delta y>0$.

The weight conclusions follow from $L_\delta\ge0$.
For the final obstruction use the flat query and one baseline attaining
response of share $\delta$, with mean orthogonal to $v$.
For every real $t>0$ its risk change equals
$-K_\delta t+L_\delta t^2\ge0$. The endpoint supremum is at least
this response's risk. Thus it cannot fall below the baseline supremum.
head: environment

label: thm:general-sensitivity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:general-sensitivity}
Fix a full-column-rank $X\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, an SPD target $A_0$,
a fixed PSD physical query $W$, and $d\le s<m$.
Put $\epsilon=\|HA_0^{-1/2}\|_F$ and recompute the Full fit, calibrated
penalty, determinant law and selected fit at $X+H$.
The explicit constants in \eqref{eq:radius-constants}--\eqref{eq:explicit-eta}
give, for $\epsilon\le r_0$,
\[
 \|M_s(X+H,W)-M_s(X,W)\|\le\eta_s(\epsilon)\le\mathcal M_s\epsilon,
 \qquad |h_s(X+H,W)-h_s(X,W)|\le\eta_s(\epsilon).
\]
For every fixed nonzero raw response,
$e^{-2\epsilon}\le J_0(X+H,y)/J_0(X,y)\le e^{2\epsilon}$.
These constants require no enumeration of row subsets.
head: environment
name: Sensitivity of the fully recalibrated procedure

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $Z=XA_0^{-1/2}$, $V=A_0^{-1/2}WA_0^{-1/2}$ and
$P=A_0^{-1/2}R_sA_0^{-1/2}$. Along the feature segment, use the explicit
Gram box $[\ell,u]$ and constants of Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}.
Calibration has marked-set activation means
$\rho_j=\lambda_j/(1+\lambda_j)$ and odds $q_j=\lambda_j/p_j$.
Its log-coordinate Hessian is $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf1_J)$.
Select $s$ slots with weights $1+q_j$ on feature slots and one on the
others, then independently mark a selected feature slot with probability
$q_j/(1+q_j)$. Conditional variance gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf1_J)\succeq
 \operatorname{diag}\{\rho_j/(1+q_j)\}\succeq\kappa_sI.
\]
The explicit $\kappa_s>0$ in \eqref{eq:calibration-modulus} follows
from the penalty sandwich and slot inclusion bounds.
Integrating this Hessian bound along a coordinate swap bounds the
spectral divided differences as well. Thus it includes all symmetric
matrix directions and repeated eigenvalues. Inverting the moment
map gives $\|\dot P\|_F\le L_X\epsilon$.

For $F_S=(Z^\top D_SZ+P)^{-1}Z^\top D_S-(I+Z^\top Z)^{-1}Z^\top$
and $T=(I+ZZ^\top)^{1/2}$, ordered differentiation of the ridge fits
and the equation $T\dot T+\dot TT=EZ^\top+ZE^\top$ give
\[
 \|F_ST\|\le B_Ft,\qquad
 \|(F_ST)^{\boldsymbol\cdot}\|\le C_F\epsilon.
\]
The log derivative of each unnormalized determinant weight is at most
$L_p\epsilon$. The normalized endpoint laws therefore have total
variation at most $\tanh(L_p\epsilon/2)$, as proved in
\eqref{eq:law-tv}. Since the risk atom is PSD and at most
$\|V\|B_F^2t^2I$, integrating its derivative and changing its law yield
\[
 \|M_s(X+H)-M_s(X)\|
 \le\|V\|\{2B_FtC_F\epsilon+
           B_F^2t^2\tanh(L_p\epsilon/2)\}=\eta_s(\epsilon).
\]
The Rayleigh principle gives the sharp-value bound.
Finally $K=(I+ZZ^\top)^{-1}$ obeys
$|\partial_x\log(y^\top Ky)|\le2\epsilon$ along the segment,
using $\|K^{1/2}Z\|\le1$ and $\|K^{1/2}\|\le1$.
Integration gives the loss ratio. Appendix~\ref{app:transfer} supplies
the stated constants and each derivative and likelihood bound.
head: environment

label: thm:transfer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:transfer}
Let $X_0$ be a balanced design as in Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-geometry},
and fix nonzero $W\succeq0$. Let $\mathcal E$ be its complete maximizing
raw response space. For each $d\le s<nd$, there are explicit positive
constants $r,L_s,v,\gamma_s$ such that, for
$\epsilon=\lVert HA_0^{-1/2}\rVert_F\le r$, all recalibrated objects
exist and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:operator-lipschitz}
 \lVert M_s(X_0+H)-M_s(X_0)\rVert\le\eta_s(\epsilon)
 \le L_s\epsilon.
\end{equation}
Here $\gamma_s$ is the gap below the full top eigenspace at $X_0$.
If $\eta_s<\gamma_s/2$ and $\omega=v\epsilon<1$, put
\[
 \theta_s=\frac{\eta_s}{\gamma_s-\eta_s}+\frac{\omega}{1-\omega}.
\]
Then $|h_s(X_0+H)-h_s(X_0)|\le\eta_s$ and
\begin{align}\label{eq:raw-regret}
 0\le{}&h_s(X_0+H)
 -\sup_{0\ne y\in\mathcal E}
 \frac{y^\top C_s(X_0+H)y}{y^\top K_{X_0+H}y}\nonumber\\
 \le{}&(h_s(X_0)+\eta_s)\min\{1,\theta_s^2\}.
\end{align}
One positive radius makes these conditions hold at every stated budget.
head: environment
name: Recalibrated transfer

label: thm:enlarged
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:enlarged}
Keep the balanced base, target and fixed physical query, and recalibrate
exactly at $X_1=X_0+H$. Write $K_1=K_{X_1}$,
$M_1=K_1^{-1/2}C_s(X_1,W)K_1^{-1/2}$ and $h_1=\lambda_{\max}(M_1)$.
Use the finite surrogate $\widetilde M$ and error $e=e_{\rm end}$ from
\eqref{eq:common-surrogate}--\eqref{eq:endpoint-error-bound}, or any valid
symmetric surrogate with $\|M_1-\widetilde M\|\le e$.
Let $U$ and $Q$ be orthonormal bases of $K_1^{1/2}\mathcal E_I$ and its
orthogonal complement. Define
\[
 a=\lambda_{\max}(U^\top\widetilde M U),\quad
 d_0=\lambda_{\max}(Q^\top\widetilde M Q),\quad
 b=\|Q^\top\widetilde M U\|,\quad g=a-d_0-2e,\quad B=b+e.
\]
If $h_{1,I}$ is the supremum over nonzero raw $y\in\mathcal E_I$ with
the endpoint loss denominator, then, when $g>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:enlarged-regret}
 0\le h_1-h_{1,I}\le
 \frac{2B^2}{\sqrt{g^2+4B^2}+g}\le\frac{B^2}{g}.
\end{equation}
At every endpoint an alternative bound is
$h_1-h_{1,I}\le\lambda_{\max}(\widetilde M)-a+2e$.
Every response of true sharp deficit $h_1-r_1(y)\le\rho$, where
$r_1(y)=y^\top C_s(X_1,W)y/(y^\top K_1y)$, obeys, if $g>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:enlarged-leakage}
 \min_{v\in\mathcal E_I}
 \sqrt{\frac{(y-v)^\top K_1(y-v)}{y^\top K_1y}}
 \le\min\left\{1,\frac{B+\sqrt{B^2+g\rho}}{g}\right\}.
\end{equation}
For an exact maximizer the sharper bound is $B/\sqrt{g^2+B^2}$.
For the full contrast space, one explicit positive feature radius works
for all nonzero PSD queries after normalization $\max_jW_{jj}=1$, and
all budgets $d\le s<m$. On that ball the regret is $O(\epsilon^2)$ and
the leakage is $O(\epsilon+\sqrt\rho)$, uniformly over those queries and
budgets. The same holds for each fixed threshold $\vartheta>0$ with
its query-dependent space $\mathcal E_{I_\vartheta}$.

name: Enlarged contrast-space transfer

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A=\lambda_{\max}(U^\top M_1U)$,
$D=\lambda_{\max}(Q^\top M_1Q)$ and $b_1=\|Q^\top M_1U\|$.
Compression and the variational principle give $A-D\ge g$ and $b_1\le B$.
For a unit vector $x=Uu+Qv$,
\[
 x^\top M_1x\le A\|u\|^2+D\|v\|^2+2b_1\|u\|\|v\|.
\]
The largest eigenvalue of the corresponding two-by-two matrix, minus
$A$, is $2b_1^2/(\sqrt{(A-D)^2+4b_1^2}+A-D)$.
It decreases with the gap and increases with the cross norm. This proves
\eqref{eq:enlarged-regret}, the classical block Rayleigh bound
\citep{lili2005}. Weyl's inequality proves the alternative bound.
Here $A=h_{1,I}$ because the trial space is $K_1^{1/2}\mathcal E_I$.

For leakage put $t=\|v\|$. Since $h_1\ge A$,
\[
 h_1-x^\top M_1x\ge(A-D)t^2-2b_1t\sqrt{1-t^2}\ge gt^2-2Bt.
\]
Solving this quadratic proves \eqref{eq:enlarged-leakage}.
For a top eigenvector, its complementary eigen-equation gives
$(h_1-D)t\le b_1\sqrt{1-t^2}$, proving the sharper bound, including ties.
A surrogate deficit at most $r$ implies true deficit at most $r+2e$.
Thus the leakage statement also has an evaluable surrogate test.

For the uniform claim, Appendix~\ref{app:enlarged} proves
$\|M_1-M_0\|\le Lh$ and $e\le\bar e(h)=O(h^2)$, with
$h=\epsilon+\|P_1-P_0\|$ and constants independent of normalized $W$.
It bounds the moving-space projector by $f(h)=O(h)$ and proves
\[
 g\ge\gamma-(\alpha_s+\gamma)f(h)^2-2Lh-4\bar e(h),\quad
 B\le Lh+2\alpha_sf(h)+2\bar e(h).
\]
The explicit dyadic choice \eqref{eq:enlarged-dyadic} makes
$g\ge\gamma/2>0$ on a whole ball. The full-space gap is
$\gamma=\alpha_s-\beta_s$, or use the threshold gap above.
Exact calibration sensitivity gives $h\le(1+L_{X,s})\epsilon$.
The finite minimum \eqref{eq:enlarged-feature-radius} then proves the
common feature radius, quadratic regret and leakage orders.
